fields.definition: A synthesis technique that produces a continuous, gradual transition between two or more source waveforms by interpolating between their shapes over time, so the timbre changes smoothly from one waveform to another.
fields.plain_english: It slowly blends one sound wave into another, the way one photo can fade into a different photo. As it blends, the tone changes little by little.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to create evolving, moving timbres from a small set of stored waveforms, giving a synth sound life and change without switching abruptly between fixed tones.
fields.practical_application: A technician modulates a morph or wavetable-position control with an envelope or LFO to make a pad or lead slowly shift from a dull, soft tone to a bright, harmonically rich one.
common_mistakes: Confusing morphing with a simple volume crossfade of two separate oscillators; true morphing interpolates the waveform shape itself, not just the loudness of two sounds.
Assuming morphing always sounds smooth, when large differences between source waveforms can produce audible stepping or harsh artifacts.
Thinking morphing and wavetable-position sweeps are unrelated, when sweeping through a wavetable is one common way morphing is implemented.
scenario_contexts: Automating a slow timbral sweep on a pad so it evolves from a soft, sine-like tone to a bright, edgy one.
Using an LFO or envelope to morph an oscillator's shape and add movement to a lead sound.
Designing evolving textures in a soft synth such as Serum or Massive by moving through morphing waveforms.

sources: Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Puckette, The Theory and Technique of Electronic Music

fields.definition: A synthesis technique, also called waveshaping, in which a signal is passed through a nonlinear transfer function that reshapes its waveform and adds new harmonics, changing the timbre in a controlled, level-dependent way.
fields.plain_english: It bends a sound wave into a new shape to give it a richer, buzzier tone. Think of it like reshaping clay to change how it looks.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to add harmonics and character to a simple tone, letting a plain waveform become a complex, brighter, or more saturated sound without extra oscillators.
fields.practical_application: A technician routes a clean synth tone through a waveshaper or saturation stage to add warmth, grit, or harmonic edge, adjusting drive to control how much new harmonic content appears.
common_mistakes: Confusing waveshaping with filtering; a filter removes harmonics, while waveshaping adds new ones through a nonlinear transfer function.
Driving the shaper too hard and creating harsh aliasing, especially at high pitches when no oversampling is used.
Assuming waveshaping only means heavy distortion, when gentle shaping can add subtle warmth and low-level harmonics.
scenario_contexts: Adding harmonic richness and grit to a synth bass by routing it through a waveshaper.
Using a soft-clipping waveshaper to emulate analog saturation on a track.
Building complex timbres from a simple sine wave by shaping it with a nonlinear curve.

sources: Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Puckette, The Theory and Technique of Electronic Music

fields.definition: An oscillator that generates sound by repeatedly reading through a stored table of single-cycle waveforms, looping the table at a rate set by the desired pitch, and often sweeping across successive waveforms to change timbre over time.
fields.plain_english: It makes sound by playing through a list of stored wave shapes, one after another. Sweeping through the list slowly changes the tone, like flipping the pages of a flip book.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to produce a wide range of rich, evolving digital timbres efficiently, using stored waveforms instead of computing complex tones in real time.
fields.practical_application: A technician selects a wavetable and modulates its position with an envelope or LFO to make a lead, bass, or pad move through different tones as a note plays.
common_mistakes: Thinking a wavetable holds a full recording, when each slot usually stores just one single-cycle waveform.
Sweeping the table position too fast and getting clicks or aliasing instead of smooth movement.
Confusing wavetable synthesis with sample playback; a wavetable oscillator loops short cycles at pitch rather than playing a whole recorded sample.
scenario_contexts: Creating an evolving lead by modulating the wavetable position with an envelope.
Programming a bright, digital pad in a synth such as Serum, Massive, or a Waldorf instrument.
Layering two detuned wavetable oscillators for a fat, moving sound.

sources: Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Puckette, The Theory and Technique of Electronic Music

fields.definition: In a sampler, the assignment of samples to defined ranges of the keyboard (key zones) and playing dynamics (velocity zones) so that the correct sample plays for a given note and how hard it is struck.
fields.plain_english: It tells a sampler which recorded sound to play for each key and how hard you press. So low keys, high keys, and soft or loud hits can each trigger their own sample.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so one instrument can cover a full keyboard and dynamic range with many samples, keeping each sample near its natural pitch and loudness instead of stretching one sound over everything.
fields.practical_application: A technician building a sampled instrument drags samples onto key and velocity ranges, sets each sample's root key, and checks that zones cover the whole keyboard with no gaps or unwanted overlaps.
common_mistakes: Leaving gaps between key zones so some notes trigger no sample and play silence.
Overlapping velocity zones by mistake so two samples sound at once at certain velocities.
Forgetting to set a sample's root key, so its zone plays back at the wrong pitch.
scenario_contexts: Building a multisampled piano by mapping each recorded note across a small range of keys.
Setting up velocity zones so soft hits trigger a quiet sample and hard hits trigger a bright, loud one.
Mapping a drum kit so each key or pad triggers a different drum sample.
